synthesis.scalar-kasner-wall-is-reduced-.formal:
Write $\Cl(1,4)$ for the algebra generated by $\Cl(1,3)$ ($e_0^2 = 1$, $e_i^2 = -1$) and one more vector $e_4$ orthogonal to it with $e_4^2 = -1$, $B_a = e_0e_a$, and let $K_5 = \{P \in \R^4 : \sum_a P_a = 1 = \sum_a P_a^2\}$, the five-dimensional Kasner sphere, and $D_s = \{(p, c) \in \R^3\times\R : \sum_i p_i = 1,\ \sum_i p_i^2 + c^2 = 1\}$. For $P \in K_5$ put $k = 1 + P_4/2$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Reduction.)} The five-dimensional synchronous gravitational field on flat $\R^{1,4}$ (the Definition's $d$-dimensional clause) with $\hb^{-1}(e_0) = e_0$, $\hb^{-1}(e_a) = T^{P_a}e_a$ ($P \in K_5$), whose derived metric is the vacuum Kasner metric $G = dT^2 - \sum_{a=1}^{4}T^{2P_a}(dx^a)^2$, is Ricci-flat ($\mathcal{R}(a) = 0$), and $G = T^{-P_4}g - T^{2P_4}(dx^4)^2$ with
\[
g = T^{P_4}\Bigl(dT^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{3}T^{2P_i}(dx^i)^2\Bigr), \qquad \phi = \sqrt{\tfrac{3}{16\pi G}}\;P_4\log T .
\]
The pair $(g, \phi)$, read as the derived metric of a diagonal synchronous gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) and a massless scalar, solves the Einstein-scalar equations exactly: in the store's sign $\mathcal{R}(a) = -8\pi G\,(a\cdot\hat\nabla\phi)\,\hat\nabla\phi$ with $\hat\nabla\phi = \hb^{T}(\nabla\phi)$ the physical gradient, and $D\cdot\hat\nabla\phi = 0$ (in components $\Ric = -8\pi G\,d\phi\otimes d\phi$ and $\Box\phi = 0$). In the proper time $\tau = T^{k}/k$ of $g$, $g = d\tau^2 - \sum_i k^{2p_i}\tau^{2p_i}(dx^i)^2$ and $\phi = q\log\tau + \mathrm{const}$ with
\[
p_i = \frac{P_i + P_4/2}{k}, \qquad 8\pi G\,q^2 = \frac{3P_4^2}{2k^2},
\]
the Kasner-disk relations $\sum_i p_i = 1$, $\sum_i p_i^2 = 1 - 8\pi G q^2$ of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.unit-boost-residue-needs-nonpositive-exponent}(iii) holding exactly.
\item \emph{(Bijection.)} $\Pi(P) = \bigl(p,\ \sqrt{3/2}\,P_4/k\bigr)$ maps $K_5$ bijectively onto $D_s$, with inverse $P_4 = c/(\sqrt{3/2} - c/2)$, $P_i = p_ik - P_4/2$; here $c = \sqrt{8\pi G}\,q$ with the sign of $P_4$. So every Einstein-scalar Kasner wall of this diagonal form is the reduction of exactly one five-dimensional vacuum Kasner wall, the scalar's rate being the fifth exponent.
\item \emph{(The completed residue.)} With $B_w = \sum_i p_iB_i$ (minus the residue of the Kasner pole, Proposition \claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-datum-kasner-wall}(i)) and $\sum_i p_i = 1$, the bivector $\hat B = B_w + c\,B_4$ satisfies $\hat B^2 = \sum_i p_i^2 + c^2$, so $\hat B$ is a unit boost of $\Cl(1,4)$ exactly when the Einstein-scalar equations hold at the wall; its $B_4$ component is the scalar's logarithmic rate and $1 - B_w^2 = c^2$. The five-dimensional residue $B_5 = \sum_a P_aB_a$ is a unit boost, and
\[
k\,B_w = \sum_{i=1}^{3}P_iB_i + \frac{P_4}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{3}B_i :
\]
the four-dimensional residue is the spatial part of $B_5$ plus the isotropic residue of the Weyl factor $T^{P_4}$, rescaled by the change of time $d\tau/dT = T^{P_4/2}$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.scalar-kasner-wall-is-reduced-.technical: The residue-sense forcing half reads the field equations at a Kasner wall as the statement that the residue of the connection's pole is a unit boost; with a massless scalar the residue squares to $1 - 8\pi Gq^2$, which raised the question whether matter is excluded at the wall or needs a new kind of wall datum. For the massless scalar (equivalently a stiff fluid) the answer is neither. A five-dimensional vacuum Kasner metric with exponents $P_1, \dots, P_4$ reduces along its fourth axis, in the Einstein frame, to a four-dimensional Kasner gravitational field with a massless scalar whose rate is fixed by $P_4$; the map from the five-dimensional Kasner sphere to the Einstein-scalar Kasner sphere $\{\sum p = 1, \sum p^2 + 8\pi G q^2 = 1\}$ is a bijection, so every diagonal Einstein-scalar Kasner wall arises this way exactly once. In the store's language the four-dimensional residue $B_w$, a boost of norm below one, completes to the unit boost $B_w + \sqrt{8\pi G}\,q\,e_0e_4$ of $\Cl(1,4)$, and the field equations at the wall are again the single statement that the completed residue is a unit boost. The relation to the five-dimensional residue is explicit: $B_w$ is its spatial part plus the isotropic pole of the conformal factor, divided by the change of time. The facts behind the reduction are standard; what is new is that the store's unit-boost reading survives matter of this kind by adding one generator. The checks verify Ricci-flatness in five dimensions, the reduced Einstein-scalar equations, the exponent map and its inverse, and the residue identities in $\Cl(1,4)$, exactly at three rational points of the five-dimensional Kasner sphere with a control off it.
synthesis.scalar-kasner-wall-is-reduced-.lay: Near the singularity inside a black hole or at the Big Bang, the series describes the gravitational field by a few exponents, and the laws of gravity become a single condition on them: a certain algebraic object, the residue, must have unit size. Adding the simplest kind of matter, a massless field, breaks that: the residue comes out smaller than one, which seemed to mean that matter needs its own special treatment at the singularity. This result shows it does not. The same situation is exactly what one sees in four dimensions when a matter-free gravitational field lives in five dimensions and one direction is hidden. In an algebra with one more generator the residue has unit size again, and the missing part of its size is precisely how fast the matter field grows near the singularity. Nothing here claims that a fifth dimension exists; it is a bookkeeping device that makes the matter fit the series' rule.

proofs.main:
Read in Gauge Theory Gravity, the metrics below are derived metrics of synchronous gravitational fields on flat spacetime (in five dimensions by the Definition's $d$-dimensional clause), and the Ricci tensors are the components of the Ricci maps of their field strengths (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}(iv)); the check computes in those components, as follows. Curvature is computed with $\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc} = \frac12 g^{ad}(\partial_{b}g_{dc} + \partial_{c}g_{db} - \partial_{d}g_{bc})$, $R^{a}{}_{bcd} = \partial_{c}\Gamma^{a}{}_{db} - \partial_{d}\Gamma^{a}{}_{cb} + \Gamma^{a}{}_{ce}\Gamma^{e}{}_{db} - \Gamma^{a}{}_{de}\Gamma^{e}{}_{cb}$, $\Ric_{bd} = R^{a}{}_{bad}$; this formula gives $\Ric = -\Lambda g$ on de Sitter in signature $(1,3)$, so the store's Ricci tensor is its negative, the calibration of Proposition \claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-datum-kasner-wall}(ii), in which a massless scalar enters as $\Ric = -8\pi G\,d\phi\otimes d\phi$ (the focusing sign; Proposition \claimref{synthesis.unit-boost-residue-needs-nonpositive-exponent}(iii) uses the same normalisation, kinetic term $\frac12(\partial\phi)^{2}$).

\emph{(1) Reduction.} For the synchronous field $\hb^{-1}(e_{0}) = e_{0}$, $\hb^{-1}(e_{a}) = T^{P_{a}}e_{a}$ with $n$ spatial directions (derived metric $dT^{2} - \sum_{a=1}^{n}T^{2P_{a}}(dx^{a})^{2}$) the computation of Proposition \claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-datum-kasner-wall}(i), (ii), which is plane by plane and holds for any $n$, gives the store-sign Ricci map $T^{2}\mathcal{R}(e_{0}) = (\sum_a P_a^{2} - \sum_a P_a)\,e_{0}$ and $T^{2}\mathcal{R}(e_{a}) = P_{a}(\sum_b P_b - 1)\,e_{a}$ (in components $T^{2}\Ric_{00}$ and $-T^{2}\Ric_{aa}$), so the field is Ricci-flat exactly when $\sum P_a = 1 = \sum P_a^{2}$; for $n = 4$ this is $P \in K_{5}$. The identity $G = T^{-P_4}g - T^{2P_4}(dx^4)^2$ is immediate from the definition of $g$. For $g = T^{P_4}(dT^{2} - \sum_{i}T^{2P_i}(dx^{i})^{2})$ the conformal factor $T^{P_4}$ and the exponents give, by the same diagonal computation, $\Ric_{ii} \propto (\sum_i P_i + P_4 - 1) = 0$ and, in the store's sign, $T^{2}\Ric_{TT} = -\frac32 P_4^{2}$ when $P \in K_{5}$, which equals $-8\pi G\,T^{2}(\partial_{T}\phi)^{2}$ for $\phi = \sqrt{3/16\pi G}\,P_4\log T$; the check computes all components exactly at three rational points of $K_{5}$ and shows that the relation fails at a point with $\sum P_a = 1$ off $K_{5}$. The wave equation: $\sqrt{|g|} = T^{(4P_4 + 2\sum_i P_i)/2} = T^{1 + P_4}$ and $g^{TT} = T^{-P_4}$, so $\sqrt{|g|}\,g^{TT}\partial_T\log T = 1$ and $\Box\phi = 0$ exactly. For the proper time, $d\tau = T^{P_4/2}dT$ gives $\tau = T^{k}/k$, $T = (k\tau)^{1/k}$, so $T^{P_4 + 2P_i} = (k\tau)^{2p_i}$ with $p_i = (P_i + P_4/2)/k$, and $\phi = \sqrt{3/16\pi G}\,(P_4/k)\log(k\tau)$, so $q = \sqrt{3/16\pi G}\,P_4/k$ and $8\pi Gq^{2} = \frac{3P_4^{2}}{2k^{2}}$. Then $\sum_i p_i = (1 - P_4 + \frac32 P_4)/k = 1$, and for any $P$ with $\sum_a P_a = 1$ and $S_2 := \sum_a P_a^{2}$,
\[
k^{2}\Bigl(\sum_i p_i^{2} + \tfrac32\tfrac{P_4^{2}}{k^{2}}\Bigr) = (S_2 - P_4^{2}) + P_4(1 - P_4) + \tfrac34P_4^{2} + \tfrac32P_4^{2} = S_2 - 1 + k^{2},
\]
so $\sum_i p_i^{2} + 8\pi Gq^{2} = 1 + (S_2 - 1)/k^{2}$, which is $1$ exactly on $K_{5}$.

\emph{(2) Bijection.} On $K_{5}$ every $|P_a| \le 1$, so $k \in [\frac12, \frac32]$ is positive and $\Pi$ is defined; by (1) it lands in $D_s$. On $D_s$, $|c| \le 1 < 2\sqrt{3/2}$, so $P_4 = c/(\sqrt{3/2} - c/2)$ is defined and is the unique solution of $c\,(1 + P_4/2) = \sqrt{3/2}\,P_4$; then $P_i = p_ik - P_4/2$ is forced by the formula for $p_i$, so $\Pi$ is injective. Given $(p, c) \in D_s$, define $P$ this way; then $\sum_a P_a = k\sum_i p_i - \frac32P_4 + P_4 = k - P_4/2 = 1$, and the identity of (1) with $\sum_i p_i^{2} + c^{2} = 1$ gives $S_2 = 1$, so $P \in K_{5}$ and $\Pi(P) = (p, c)$: $\Pi$ is surjective.

\emph{(3) The completed residue.} In $\Cl(1,4)$ the bivectors $B_a = e_0e_a$ ($a = 1, \dots, 4$) square to $-e_0^{2}e_a^{2} = 1$ and anticommute pairwise (for $a \neq b$, $B_aB_b = -e_0^{2}e_ae_b = -e_ae_b$ is antisymmetric in $a, b$), so $(\sum_a x_aB_a)^{2} = \sum_a x_a^{2}$. Hence $\hat B^{2} = \sum_i p_i^{2} + c^{2}$ and $B_5^{2} = \sum_a P_a^{2} = 1$; by Proposition \claimref{synthesis.unit-boost-residue-needs-nonpositive-exponent}(iii), given $\sum_i p_i = 1$, the Einstein-scalar equations at the wall hold exactly when $\sum_i p_i^{2} = 1 - 8\pi Gq^{2}$, that is when $\hat B^{2} = 1$, and then $1 - B_w^{2} = c^{2}$. Finally $k\,p_i = P_i + P_4/2$ is the displayed identity read coefficientwise on $B_1, B_2, B_3$; the term $\frac{P_4}{2}\sum_iB_i$ is the residue contributed by the factor $T^{P_4}$, since for $\Omega^{2}\tilde g$ with $\Omega^{2} = T^{P_4}$ the boost block of the Levi-Civita connection in the rescaled orthonormal frame acquires $\partial_T\log\Omega = P_4/(2T)$ on each spatial leg (the standard conformal change of the connection one-forms), and the factor $k$ is the conversion from $1/T$ in the frame of $\tilde g$ to $1/\tau$ in that of $g$ ($\tau^{-1}d\tau = k\,T^{-1}dT$). The check verifies the squares and the coefficient identity with GA.py in $\Cl(1,4)$ (with $e_4^{2} = -\frac32$ for $\hat B$, which absorbs $\sqrt{3/2}$ so that the coefficient $P_4/k$ is rational, and $e_4^{2} = -1$ for $B_5$). $\square$

synthesis.tangential-derivative-transpor.formal:
Let the gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on the collar of flat spacetime be admissible (Definition \claimref{obj.interior.weighted-blow-up-hubble-normalisation-admissible}), $K \subset \mathcal{B}$ compact, and $\{\gamma_{y}\}_{|y| < y_{0}}$ a family of tangential curves at time $\tau$ inside $K$, each parametrised by Hubble-normalised arclength on $[0, \lambda]$, with $(y, s) \mapsto \gamma_{y}(s)$ of class $C^{1}$ and unit directions $u_{y}(s)$ differentiable in $y$, $|\partial_{y}u_{y}(s)| \le c_{2}$. Suppose $E_{\tau}$ is $C^{1}$ along $\mathcal{B}$ on $K$, put $\varepsilon := \|E_{\tau}\|_{K}$, and let
\[
\delta \;:=\; \sup_{y,\,s}\bigl\|\partial_{y}\bigl(E_{\tau}(\gamma_{y}(s))[u_{y}(s)]\bigr)\bigr\|
\]
be the derivative of the error along the family. Let $T_{y}$, $T^{0}_{y}$ be the transports along $\gamma_{y}$ of the Hubble-normalised rotation-gauge field (its $D$-transport) and of the Kasner model $-\sum_{i}p_{i}B_{i}\otimes\hat\theta^{i}$ (Theorem \claimref{interior.weighted-limit-theorem}(3)). Then
\[
\bigl\|\partial_{y}T_{y}(\lambda) - \partial_{y}T^{0}_{y}(\lambda)\bigr\| \;\le\; e^{\lambda(1 + \varepsilon)}\bigl(\lambda\,\delta + \varepsilon\,c_{2}\,\lambda^{2}\bigr).
\]
If $\|dE_{\tau}\| \le \varepsilon_{1}$ along unit tangential vectors and $\|\partial_{y}\gamma_{y}\| \le c_{1}$ in Hubble-normalised length, then $\delta \le \varepsilon_{1}c_{1} + \varepsilon c_{2}$. For a coordinate family, in which $y$ moves the base point along a coordinate $x$ of $\mathcal{B}$ with the curves' directions fixed ($c_{2} = 0$), $\delta = \sup_{K}\|\partial_{x}E_{\tau}[u]\|$, the coordinate derivative of the error, and the bound is $\lambda\,\delta\,e^{\lambda(1 + \varepsilon)}$. Consequently, if $\delta(\tau) \to 0$ as $\tau \to 0$, then with Theorem \claimref{interior.transport-level-convergence-along-tangential-curves} $T_{y}(\lambda) \to T^{0}_{y}(\lambda)$ in $C^{1}$ in $y$, uniformly over families with given $\lambda$ and $c_{2}$, and the limiting transport is $C^{1}$ in $y$ with the Kasner model's derivative. The decay clauses of admissibility do not imply $\delta(\tau) \to 0$; the result is conditional on it.
synthesis.tangential-derivative-transpor.technical:
The tangential convergence theorem compares the transport of the Hubble-normalised connection with the Kasner model's along a single curve at time $\tau$. Edge regularity asks how that comparison varies as the curve moves. Differentiating the two transport equations along a one-parameter family of curves gives a linear equation for the difference of the derivatives, driven by three terms: the error times the model's derivative, the derivative of the error along the family, and the change of the model generator with the curve's direction times the already-controlled difference of the transports. Variation of constants and Gronwall bound it by $e^{\lambda(1+\varepsilon)}(\lambda\delta + \varepsilon c_{2}\lambda^{2})$, where $\varepsilon$ is the size of the admissibility error, $\delta$ the size of its derivative along the family, and $c_{2}$ how fast the curves' directions turn.

For families that move the base point in a coordinate, which is what regularity of the boundary data concerns, $\delta$ is the coordinate derivative of the error. So the derivatives converge whenever that coordinate derivative tends to zero. Admissibility as written does not say this, and its decay clauses cannot: an error that decays while oscillating ever faster has a coordinate derivative that blows up. The remaining edge-regularity question is therefore exactly a decay statement for the coordinate derivative of the error, to be established, or assumed, for the general admissible gravitational field.
synthesis.tangential-derivative-transpor.lay: Near the singularity, the framework compares how directions are carried along short paths with how they are carried in a simple model, and an earlier result showed the two agree in the limit. This result asks whether they also agree in how they change when the path is moved sideways. They do, provided the small difference between the true gravitational field and the model changes ever more slowly from place to place as the singularity is approached; if that difference wiggles faster and faster, nothing forces agreement. The question of smoothness at the edge is thereby reduced to one checkable property of that difference.

proofs.main:
Fix $\tau$ and suppress it. Along $\gamma_{y}$ write the Hubble-normalised generator as $G_{y}(s) = H_{y}(s) + \mathcal{E}_{y}(s)$, with the model part $H_{y}(s) = -\sum_{i}u^{i}_{y}(s)\,p_{i}B_{i}$ and the error $\mathcal{E}_{y}(s) = E_{\tau}(\gamma_{y}(s))[u_{y}(s)]$, as in the admissibility display of Definition \claimref{obj.interior.weighted-blow-up-hubble-normalisation-admissible}. Then $T_{y}' = G_{y}T_{y}$, $(T^{0}_{y})' = H_{y}T^{0}_{y}$, both equal to $1$ at $s = 0$. The bounds used are those of the proof of Theorem \claimref{interior.transport-level-convergence-along-tangential-curves}: $\|H_{y}\| \le 1$ (Cauchy-Schwarz with $\sum_{i}p_{i}^{2} = 1$ and $\|B_{i}\| = 1$), $\|\mathcal{E}_{y}\| \le \varepsilon$, $\|G_{y}\| \le 1 + \varepsilon$, hence $\|T_{y}(s)\| \le e^{s(1+\varepsilon)}$, $\|T^{0}_{y}(s)\| \le e^{s}$, $\|T_{y}(\lambda)T_{y}(s)^{-1}\| \le e^{(\lambda - s)(1 + \varepsilon)}$, and the theorem's own conclusion applied on $[0, s]$, $\|T_{y}(s) - T^{0}_{y}(s)\| \le s\,\varepsilon\,e^{s(1+\varepsilon)}$.

\emph{Derivative bounds.} The generators are $C^{1}$ in $y$: $\partial_{y}H_{y} = -\sum_{i}(\partial_{y}u^{i}_{y})p_{i}B_{i}$, so $\|\partial_{y}H_{y}\| \le |\partial_{y}u_{y}| \le c_{2}$ by Cauchy-Schwarz again, and $\partial_{y}\mathcal{E}_{y} = dE_{\tau}(\partial_{y}\gamma_{y})[u_{y}] + E_{\tau}(\gamma_{y})[\partial_{y}u_{y}]$, so $\|\partial_{y}\mathcal{E}_{y}\| = \delta$ at most by definition, and $\delta \le \varepsilon_{1}c_{1} + \varepsilon c_{2}$ when $\|dE_{\tau}\| \le \varepsilon_{1}$ and $\|\partial_{y}\gamma_{y}\| \le c_{1}$, using linearity of $E_{\tau}$ in the direction. For a coordinate family the first term is $\partial_{x}E_{\tau}[u]$ times $\partial_{y}x = 1$ and the second vanishes, so $\delta$ is the coordinate derivative of the error; in Hubble-normalised length a coordinate displacement has $c_{1}$ growing like a negative power of $\tau$, which is why the hypothesis is stated through $\delta$ and not through $\varepsilon_{1}$ and $c_{1}$ separately. By differentiable dependence of solutions of linear equations on parameters, $D := \partial_{y}T_{y}$ and $D^{0} := \partial_{y}T^{0}_{y}$ exist and solve $D' = GD + (\partial_{y}G)T$, $(D^{0})' = HD^{0} + (\partial_{y}H)T^{0}$, with $D(0) = D^{0}(0) = 0$. For the model, variation of constants gives $D^{0}(s) = \int_{0}^{s}T^{0}(s)T^{0}(\sigma)^{-1}(\partial_{y}H)(\sigma)T^{0}(\sigma)\,d\sigma$, and since $\|T^{0}(s)T^{0}(\sigma)^{-1}\| \le e^{s - \sigma}$ and $\|T^{0}(\sigma)\| \le e^{\sigma}$, $\|D^{0}(s)\| \le c_{2}\,s\,e^{s}$.

\emph{The difference.} $X := D - D^{0}$ satisfies
\[
X' \;=\; G X \;+\; \mathcal{E}\,D^{0} \;+\; (\partial_{y}\mathcal{E})\,T \;+\; (\partial_{y}H)\,(T - T^{0}), \qquad X(0) = 0,
\]
as one sees by subtracting the two derivative equations and writing $G D - H D^{0} = G X + (G - H)D^{0}$ and $(\partial_{y}G)T - (\partial_{y}H)T^{0} = (\partial_{y}\mathcal{E})T + (\partial_{y}H)(T - T^{0})$. Variation of constants gives $X(\lambda) = \int_{0}^{\lambda}T(\lambda)T(s)^{-1}\,[\cdots](s)\,ds$, and the bracket is bounded by $\varepsilon c_{2}s e^{s} + \delta\,e^{s(1+\varepsilon)} + c_{2}\,s\,\varepsilon\,e^{s(1+\varepsilon)} \le e^{s(1+\varepsilon)}\bigl(\delta + 2\varepsilon c_{2}s\bigr)$. Multiplying by $e^{(\lambda - s)(1+\varepsilon)}$ and integrating over $[0, \lambda]$ gives $\|X(\lambda)\| \le e^{\lambda(1+\varepsilon)}\bigl(\lambda\delta + \varepsilon c_{2}\lambda^{2}\bigr)$, the display. For $c_{2} = 0$ only the $\lambda\delta$ term survives.

\emph{Consequences.} The right side depends on the family only through $\lambda$ and $c_{2}$, and on the metric only through $\varepsilon(\tau)$ and $\delta(\tau)$; $\varepsilon(\tau) \to 0$ by admissibility. If $\delta(\tau) \to 0$ the right side tends to $0$; with Theorem \claimref{interior.transport-level-convergence-along-tangential-curves} this is convergence of $T_{y}(\lambda)$ to $T^{0}_{y}(\lambda)$ in $C^{1}$ in $y$, uniformly, so the limit is $C^{1}$ in $y$ with the model's derivative (uniform convergence of functions and of their derivatives). The model transport $T^{0}_{y}(\lambda)$ depends on $y$ only through the directions $u_{y}$ and the exponents of Theorem \claimref{interior.weighted-limit-theorem}(3), so its derivative is explicit. Nothing in admissibility controls $\delta$: the definition bounds $E_{\tau}$ and $\|E_{\tau}\|/\tau$ only, and an error of the form $\tau^{1/2}\varphi(x/\tau)$ with $\varphi$ bounded and $\varphi'(0) \ne 0$ meets every decay clause while its coordinate derivative at $x = 0$ is $\tau^{-1/2}\varphi'(0)$, unbounded (the sharpness example filed alongside, synthesis.admissible-decay-does-not-control-tangential-derivatives, takes $\tau^{1/2}\varphi(x/\tau^{2})$, with coordinate derivative $\tau^{-3/2}$ at $x = 0$). So the conclusion is conditional on the stated hypothesis.

\emph{The check.} The script runs the discrete (Euler-product) form of this argument in exact arithmetic on $4 \times 4$ real matrices of $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$, at the Schwarzschild exponents and at the Kasner point $(-\tfrac27, \tfrac37, \tfrac67)$: a family of curves with directions on the unit circle in its rational parametrisation and a noncommuting polynomial error field, differentiated in $y$ exactly by dual numbers. It verifies the discrete variation-of-constants identity for $T - T^{0}$ in value and in $y$-derivative, the model bound $\|H\| \le 1$ on rational unit directions in the max-row-sum norm, the chain-rule bound $\delta \le \varepsilon_{1}c_{1} + \varepsilon c_{2}$ with the four constants computed separately, and the discrete forms of both bounds, with $(1 + h(1 + \varepsilon))^{n}$ in place of $e^{\lambda(1+\varepsilon)}$. Two tightness controls show each term is needed: an error with no base-point dependence at a point where the direction is stationary has $\delta = 0$ but a nonzero derivative of the transport difference, so the $\varepsilon c_{2}\lambda^{2}$ term cannot be dropped; and over a curve of length $12$ the bound without the growth factor fails while the stated one holds.

synthesis.taub-nut-cauchy-horizon-is-tau.formal:
Let $\sigma_{1}, \sigma_{2}, \sigma_{3}$ be the left-invariant one-forms of $SU(2)$ with $d\sigma_{1} = -\sigma_{2}\wedge\sigma_{3}$ and cyclically, and let a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) have derived metric $N^{2}dT^{2} - \sum_{l}a_{l}(T)^{2}\sigma_{l}^{2}$ with $N = a_{1}a_{2}a_{3}$, physical orthonormal frame $e_{0}$, $e_{l}$ dual to $N\,dT$, $a_{l}\sigma_{l}$, $B_{l} = e_{0}e_{l}$, $I = e_{0}e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}$, $\alpha_{l} = \log a_{l}$, $C = \alpha_{1}'\alpha_{2}' + \alpha_{2}'\alpha_{3}' + \alpha_{3}'\alpha_{1}'$, and $G^{-1}(\xi, \eta) = \sum\xi_{l}\eta_{l} - \tfrac12(\sum\xi_{l})(\sum\eta_{l})$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Diagonal Bianchi IX in harmonic time.)} The field equations $\mathcal{R}(a) = 0$ hold if and only if $\alpha_{l}'' = -\sum_{m}G^{-1}_{lm}\,\partial V/\partial\alpha_{m}$ and $C = V$, with $V = \tfrac14\sum_{l}e^{4\alpha_{l}} - \tfrac12\sum_{i<j}e^{2(\alpha_{i} + \alpha_{j})}$. The rotation-gauge field has $\Omega(e_{0}) = 0$ and, with $H_{k} = \alpha_{k}'/N$ and $\mu_{i} = a_{i}/(a_{j}a_{k})$,
\[
\Omega(e_{k}) \;=\; -H_{k}B_{k} + \tfrac12(\mu_{i} + \mu_{j} - \mu_{k})\,e_{i}e_{j} \qquad ((i, j, k) \text{ cyclic}).
\]
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Taub-NUT.)} For constants $m$ and $l > 0$ put $U(t) = (-t^{2} + 2mt + l^{2})/(t^{2} + l^{2})$ and $t_{\pm} = m \pm \sqrt{m^{2} + l^{2}}$. On $t_{-} < t < t_{+}$ (where $U > 0$) the scale factors $a_{1} = a_{2} = \sqrt{t^{2} + l^{2}}$, $a_{3} = 2l\sqrt{U}$ with $dT = dt/(2lU(t^{2} + l^{2}))$ solve the equations of (i): this is the Taub region of the Taub-NUT field, with derived metric $U^{-1}dt^{2} - (2l)^{2}U\sigma_{3}^{2} - (t^{2} + l^{2})(\sigma_{1}^{2} + \sigma_{2}^{2})$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The limit at $t_{+}$.)} Let $\tau$ be the proper time to the locus $t = t_{+}$, reached at finite $\tau$, with $\tau$ increasing away from it as in Definition \claimref{obj.interior.weighted-blow-up-hubble-normalisation-admissible}. As $\tau \to 0$ the Kasner weights $\tau H_{l}$ tend to the Taub point $(0, 0, 1)$ and the Hubble-normalised values converge:
\[
\widehat\Omega_{\tau}(e_{1}),\ \widehat\Omega_{\tau}(e_{2}) \to 0, \qquad \widehat\Omega_{\tau}(e_{3}) \to -B_{3} + \kappa\,e_{1}e_{2} = -(1 - \kappa I)B_{3}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{t_{+}}{l} = \cot\frac{\varphi}{2},
\]
with $\varphi = \arg(m + Il) \in (0, \pi)$. The limit values generate the one-dimensional Lie algebra $\R(1 - \kappa I)B_{3}$, and the error relative to the Taub Kasner model $-B_{3}\otimes\hat\theta^{3}$ tends to $\kappa IB_{3}\otimes\hat\theta^{3} \neq 0$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Consequence.)} The approach never returns close to a Kasner model with $1 \le u \le 2$, and the conclusion of clause (iii) of \claimref{synthesis.bkl-bounce-invariant-holonomy-and-bound} (accumulation values generating $\Lambda^{2}W$) fails for it: the return hypothesis cannot be dropped, as the flat Kasner field $(1, 0, 0)$ of \claimref{synthesis.bkl-bounces-no-framewise-invariant}(ii) already shows; Taub-NUT is a non-flat witness. Its one-dimensional algebra is the Taub point's $\R B_{3}$ rotated by the duality factor $1 - \kappa I$, which is absent for the flat Kasner field ($\kappa I B_{3}$ is the slices' rotation term).
\end{enumerate}
The sign of $\kappa$ against $I$ depends on the orientation of $\sigma$ relative to the frame and on the sign of $l$; its magnitude does not. The locus $t = t_{+}$ is the Cauchy horizon of Taub-NUT (Misner 1963, cited from memory, not proved here and not used in (i) to (iv)).
synthesis.taub-nut-cauchy-horizon-is-tau.technical: Taub-NUT's Taub region is an exact vacuum solution with the symmetry of the three-sphere and two equal scale factors. In the synchronous gauge of its homogeneous slices the approach to $t = t_{+}$ shrinks one direction linearly while the other two stay finite, so its Kasner weights tend to the Taub point of the Kasner circle. The normalised connection converges there, but not to the flat Kasner value: on the shrinking axis it is the boost along that axis plus a rotation in the plane of the other two, a complex boost $-(1 - \kappa I)B_{3}$, because the slices' connection on that axis is of the same order as the expansion. The coefficient $\kappa$ is the cotangent of half the argument of the complex mass $m + Il$ (numbers are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I\}$, $I = e_{0}e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}$), so the NUT parameter appears in the limit as a duality component. One element generates a one-dimensional algebra, not $\Lambda^{2}W$; this is a second, non-flat witness, after the flat Kasner field, that the bounce-invariant holonomy result needs its return hypothesis. The locus reached is the Cauchy horizon of Taub-NUT, beyond which the field continues (cited from the literature, not proved here).
synthesis.taub-nut-cauchy-horizon-is-tau.lay: Near the special direction-pattern where only one direction collapses, the simplest model is empty flat space seen from a moving family of observers. This result looks at a genuinely curved solution, Taub-NUT, that reaches the same pattern. Its rescaled gravitational field settles to a boost combined with a twist, where the flat model has no twist, and the size of the twist is set by the solution's two charges, its mass and its NUT parameter. The field there produces only a single transformation, not every Lorentz transformation. In the literature the place reached is a horizon beyond which spacetime continues, not a true singularity.

synthesis.tractor-transport-weak-null-cr.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) with derived metric $g$, and let $\gamma : [s_0, s_1] \to M$ be a causal worldline of $D$-parallel velocity (a causal geodesic of $g$) with affine parameter $s$, crossing at $s_c \in (s_0, s_1)$ a hypersurface across which the derived metric is continuous, smooth on either side, with no part of the Schouten tensor concentrated on the hypersurface (along $\gamma$, $\Sch(\gamma',\cdot)$ is the locally integrable function given by its values off $s_c$, with no surface layer at $s_c$), and suppose $D$-transport (the Levi-Civita transport of $g$) along $\gamma$ extends continuously across $s_c$, so that a $D$-parallel physical frame along $\gamma$ exists on $[s_0, s_1]$. Write the tractor transport along $\gamma$, the transport of the $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field $\Omega_{T}(a) = \Omega(a) - \nInf \wedge \hb^{-1}(a) + \nO \wedge \Sch(\hb^{-1}(a))$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.gtg-tractor-gauge-field-reproduces-tractor-connection}, in the splitting of the scale $g$ (Fact \claimref{interior.imported-tractor-connection}), in that frame, as $x' = A x$ with $A = E_{\gamma'} + N_{\Sch(\gamma',\cdot)}$, where $E_{\gamma'}$ is the soldering part (the term $-\nInf \wedge \hb^{-1}(x')$, $x'$ the background tangent) and, for a covector $v$, $N_v$ is the nilpotent map $(\sigma, \mu, \rho) \mapsto (0,\, \sigma v,\, -\ip{v}{\mu})$ of the nilradical $\mathfrak g_1$. Suppose
\[
\Sch(\gamma', \cdot) \;=\; S\,\nu\,n + R ,
\]
with $n$ a parallel null covector along $\gamma$, $\nu := n(\gamma') \neq 0$ (constant), $S$ a scalar function and $R$ a covector field with integrable components on $[s_0, s_1]$, and assume the Tipler-type condition $\int_{s_0}^{s_1} |s - s_c|\,|S(s)|\,ds < \infty$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Removal.)} The equation $y'' = \nu^2 S\, y$ has solutions $y$ on $[s_0, s_c)$ and on $(s_c, s_1]$, continuous and positive on $[s_0, s_1]$, with $y'$ integrable (shrinking $[s_0,s_1]$ about $s_c$ if necessary). For any such $y$ put $f := y'/(\nu y)$. In the variables $\hat x := (1 - f N_n)\,x$ the transport equation reads
\[
\hat x' \;=\; \bigl(E_{\gamma'} + N_R + f\,[E_{\gamma'}, N_n]\bigr)\,\hat x ,
\]
whose coefficient is integrable; so the transport across $s_c$ exists and is unique for each such $y$.
\item \emph{(The ambiguity is exactly one nilpotent direction.)} Two such solutions $y_1, y_2$ give transports across $s_c$ that differ by the insertion, at $s_c$, of $\exp(c N_n)$ for a real $c$, and every $c \in \R$ occurs. The transport through the crossing is therefore defined exactly modulo the one-parameter subgroup $\exp(\R N_n)$ of the nilradical attached to the conormal $n$.
\item \emph{(Divergence in the metric's scale.)} If $S$ has a fixed sign near $s_c$ and is not integrable on a side of $s_c$, then $f$ is unbounded there, and in the splitting of $g$ (or of any scale differing from it by a bounded change of splitting) a parallel tractor has bounded components up to $s_c$ only if $\sigma(s_c) = 0$ and $\ip{n}{\mu(s_c)} = 0$: the divergence is in the $\mathfrak g_1$ slot along $n$. If instead $S$ is integrable, $A$ itself is integrable, the transport across is unique, and it is the one given by the solutions $y$ whose derivative is continuous at $s_c$.
\item \emph{(Einstein sides.)} If $\mathcal{R}(a) = \Lambda a$ on both sides (for the derived metric $\Ric = \Lambda g$), then $\Sch = \tfrac12(\Ric - \tfrac{R}{6}g) = \tfrac{\Lambda}{6} g$ by the four-dimensional Schouten formula of Fact \claimref{interior.imported-tractor-connection}, $S = 0$, and tractor transport across $s_c$ exists and is unique exactly when $D$-transport does.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.tractor-transport-weak-null-cr.technical:
The question was whether the tractor connection can be integrated along causal curves through a perturbed Cauchy horizon, where the derived metric of the gravitational field is continuous but its Christoffel symbols, the connection components, are not square-integrable and the Schouten tensor blows up. The answer is a sharp form of "it fails in a nilpotent slot". Along a crossing geodesic, suppose the non-integrable part of the Schouten term is a rank-one null piece $S\nu n$ along a parallel null covector $n$ (the conormal of the crossed null hypersurface), and that $S$ obeys a Tipler-type double-integral condition. A change of splitting along $\gamma$ by the nilpotent element $f N_n$ (the one induced by a scale whose logarithm along $\gamma$ is $\log y$), with $f$ the logarithmic derivative of a solution of the Jacobi-type equation $y'' = \nu^2 S y$, removes the singular piece exactly: the transformed coefficient is integrable, so the transport across the crossing exists. The solution $y$ is continuous but its derivative diverges at the crossing, and continuing it across involves one free constant; that constant changes the transport by an element of the one-parameter group $\exp(\R N_n)$, and by nothing else. In the metric's own splitting the components blow up in exactly that direction. The hypotheses (continuous Levi-Civita transport, a rank-one null divergence along a parallel covector, the Tipler-type bound, no surface layer) are not yet confirmed for the known perturbed Cauchy-horizon solutions, whose Christoffel symbols fail to be square-integrable; that failure alone does not supply a parallel frame. In vacuum (or with a cosmological constant) the Schouten tensor is a multiple of the metric, there is no singular piece, and the tractor transport problem is that of $D$-transport.

The exact checks verify the gauge identity for fixed rational frames, causal tangents and null conormals, the two explicit frames (a null generator and a radial timelike crossing), and an explicit profile with $|S| \sim |s - s_c|^{-3/2}$, non-integrable while $|s - s_c||S|$ is integrable.
synthesis.tractor-transport-weak-null-cr.lay: Inside charged and rotating black holes there is an inner horizon where infalling radiation piles up. The gravitational field stays continuous there, but its rates of change blow up. The programme's main tool for carrying structure along a path, the tractor transport, contains one more derivative than ordinary parallel transport, so one might expect it to fail outright. This result shows it survives along a path, provided three conditions hold there: ordinary parallel transport passes the horizon, the blow-up is concentrated in a single null direction, and it is of the weak kind that leaves infalling objects with finite tidal stretching. Then, after a suitable change of description along the path, the transport goes through. Whether the known models of perturbed inner horizons meet these conditions is not yet confirmed. What is lost is a single number, a one-parameter freedom in how the transport continues past the horizon, and it sits exactly in the nilpotent part of the symmetry algebra where the series expected the damage to be.

A linear equation with integrable coefficient has, for each initial value, a unique absolutely continuous solution on $[s_0, s_1]$ (Picard iteration in the integral form, with the Gronwall bound $\|\hat x(s)\| \le \|\hat x(s_0)\|\exp\int\|\cdot\|$); so the transport across $s_c$ exists, as $x(s_1) = (1 + f(s_1)N_n)\hat T (1 - f(s_0)N_n)x(s_0)$, with $\hat T$ the transport of $\hat x$.

\emph{(2) Comparing two scales.} (Each $f = y'/(
u y)$ is a change of splitting along $\gamma$ only: it is the one induced by a scale $e^{\omega}$ with $\omega = \log y$ along $\gamma$, since $f n(\gamma') = (\log y)'$.) Let $y_1, y_2$ be admissible and $r := y_2/y_1$. On each side the Wronskian $W = y_1 y_2' - y_1' y_2$ is constant (the equation has no first-order term), so $r' = W/y_1^2$ is continuous up to $s_c$ from each side, with one-sided values $W_\pm/y_1(s_c)^2$, and $r'' = -2Wy_1'/y_1^3$ is integrable. Hence $\delta := f_2 - f_1 = r'/(
u r)$ is absolutely continuous on each closed side, with a jump $c := \delta(s_c^+) - \delta(s_c^-)$. Since $N_n^2 = 0$, $(1 + aN_n)(1 + bN_n) = 1 + (a + b)N_n$, so on each side $\hat x_2 = (1 - \delta N_n)\hat x_1$ for the solutions continued within that side. Following a solution from $s_0$: the two gauged solutions agree up to the factor $(1 - \delta N_n)$ on the left, both continue continuously across $s_c$ in their own gauges, and on the right the gauge-$2$ continuation equals $(1 - \delta N_n)$ applied to the gauge-$1$ solution with initial value $\exp(c N_n)\hat x_1(s_c)$ at $s_c$. So the two transports differ exactly by the insertion of $\exp(cN_n)$ at the crossing, in the gauge of $y_1$. Every $c$ occurs: keep $y_2 = y_1$ on the left and put $y_2 = y_1 + c'v$ on the right, on an interval $(s_c, s_1']$ shrunk, depending on $c'$, so that $y_2 > 0$ there (harmless, since transport away from $s_c$ is regular), with $v$ the solution with $v(s_c) = 0$, $v'(s_c^+) = 1$ (continuous derivative up to $s_c$, since $|v(t)| \le C|t - s_c|$ makes $Sv$ integrable). Then $W_+ = c'\,(y_1 v' - y_1' v)(s_c^+) = c'\,y_1(s_c)$, because $|y_1'(t)\,v(t)| \le C\,|t - s_c|\,(C' + \int_t^{s_1}|S|)$ tends to zero by dominated convergence against the integrable $|t' - s_c||S(t')|$; so $c = c'/(
u y_1(s_c))$ ranges over $\R$. Distinct $c$ give distinct transports, since $\exp(cN_n)$ moves every tractor with $\sigma 
eq 0$.

\emph{(3) The metric's scale.} If $S$ has a fixed sign near $s_c$ and $\int|S| = \infty$ on one side, then $y' = y'(s_0) + 
u^2\int S y$ with $y \ge 	frac12$ is monotone and unbounded there, so $|f| 	o \infty$. In the splitting of $g$, $x = (1 + fN_n)\hat x$ has components $\sigma = \hat\sigma$, $\mu = \hat\mu + f\hat\sigma\, n$, $ho = \hatho - f\ip{n}{\hat\mu}$, with $\hat x$ continuous; they stay bounded only if $\hat\sigma(s_c) = 0$ and $\ip{n}{\hat\mu}(s_c) = 0$, and $\sigma = \hat\sigma$, $\ip{n}{\mu} = \ip{n}{\hat\mu}$ because $n$ is null. A change of splitting with bounded parameters and bounded inverse preserves boundedness. If $S$ is integrable, $A$ is integrable, the transport in the splitting of $g$ exists and is unique, and $f = y'/(
u y)$ is then continuous for exactly the solutions $y$ with continuous derivative, for which $\delta$ has no jump.

\emph{(4)} If $\mathcal{R}(a) = \Lambda a$ (for the derived metric $\Ric = \Lambda g$), then $\mathcal{R} = 4\Lambda$ and the four-dimensional Schouten formula $\Sch(a) = 	frac12(\mathcal{R}(a) - 	frac16\mathcal{R}\,a)$ of Fact \claimref{interior.imported-tractor-connection} gives $\Sch(a) = 	frac12(\Lambda - 	frac{4\Lambda}{6})a = 	frac{\Lambda}{6}a$, so $\Sch(\gamma') = 	frac{\Lambda}{6}\gamma'$ is bounded and $S = 0$; then $A$ is bounded wherever the parallel frame is defined, and the only input is the continuity of that frame, which is the existence of Levi-Civita transport across $s_c$.

\emph{The no-surface-layer hypothesis.} All integrals above are of the function $\Sch(\gamma',\cdot)$ off $s_c$. A part of the Schouten tensor concentrated at $s_c$ would add a distributional term to $A$: a pure null shell $c_0\, n \otimes n$ contributes $c_0 
u N_n \delta_{s_c}$, whose effect is a further factor $\exp(c_0
u N_n)$ already contained in the ambiguity of (2), but a shell with a trace part contributes a multiple of $N_{\gamma'^{ lat}}\,\delta_{s_c}$, a jump outside $\exp(\R N_n)$; the hypothesis excludes both, and the uniqueness statements of (3) and (4) hold only under it.

\emph{In components (the earlier route).} In the slots $(\sigma, \mu, ho)$ of the splitting of $g$ the tractor connection of Fact \claimref{interior.imported-tractor-connection} reads, in the parallel frame, $\sigma' = \mu(\gamma')$, $\mu' = -\gamma'^{ lat}ho + \Sch(\gamma', \cdot)\,\sigma$, $ho' = -\ip{\Sch(\gamma', \cdot)}{\mu}$, and (a) to (c) are direct evaluations of the maps on $(\sigma, \mu, ho)$; the existing checks verify them as $6	imes 6$ matrices.

synthesis.unit-boost-residue-needs-nonpo.formal:
Let $p = (p_1, p_2, p_3) \in \R^3$ with $\sum_i p_i = 1$, and let $B_w = \sum_i p_i B_i$ with $B_i = e_0 e_i$ in $\Cl(1,3)$; the residue bivector of the Kasner pole (\claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-datum-kasner-wall}(i)), in the sign of the rotation-gauge field, is $-B_w$, which has the same square, so each statement below about $B_w$ holds for the residue.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $B_w^2 = \sum_i p_i^2$. So $B_w$ is a unit boost if and only if $p$ lies on the Kasner circle, which is the second Kasner relation of \claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-datum-kasner-wall}(ii).
\item On the Kasner circle some exponent is nonpositive, and an exponent vanishes only at the permutations of $(1,0,0)$. Equivalently, if every $p_i > 0$ then $B_w^2 = 1 - 2\sum_{i<j}p_ip_j < 1$.
\item On the synchronous diagonal Kasner field $\hb^{-1}(e_0) = e_0$, $\hb^{-1}(e_i) = \tau^{p_i}e_i$ on flat spacetime (derived metric, in components, $d\tau^2 - \sum_i \tau^{2p_i}(dx^i)^2$) coupled to a massless scalar $\phi = q\log\tau$, at leading order in $\tau$, the Einstein-scalar equations hold if and only if $\sum_i p_i = 1$ and $\sum_i p_i^2 = 1 - 8\pi G q^2$ (the scalar's kinetic term normalised as $\tfrac12 Q(\hb^{T}(\nabla\phi))$, in components $\tfrac12(\partial\phi)^2$), the wave equation then holding exactly. Hence $B_w^2 = 1 - 8\pi G q^2$: the residue is a unit boost exactly when the scalar carries no logarithmic rate.
\end{enumerate}
So the identification of step (2) of \claimref{dark-energy.forcing-half-schwarzschild-wall-residue-sense}, field equations at the wall equal to a unit-boost residue, holds only on vacuum walls, and every such wall has an exponent $p_i \leq 0$.
synthesis.unit-boost-residue-needs-nonpo.technical: The residue-sense forcing half reads the leading field equations at a Kasner wall as the statement that the residue of the connection's pole is a unit boost, which is what makes it the completion's weight. This result shows how narrow that reading is. The ingredients are standard and not new: the Kasner relations and the fact that one exponent on the Kasner circle is nonpositive (Kasner 1921; Landau and Lifshitz, vol.~2), and the Kasner disk of a massless scalar, sum of squares $1 - 8\pi G q^2$ (Belinski and Khalatnikov 1973), all cited from memory. What is added is their bearing on the store's reading: the residue squares to the sum of the squared exponents, so it is a unit boost only on the vacuum circle, where an exponent is nonpositive, and with a scalar of nonzero log-rate it is a boost of norm below one. Read against the literature (cited from memory, not imported into the store): the nonpositive exponent is exactly what destabilises a Kasner regime in generic vacuum data (Belinski, Khalatnikov and Lifshitz; Ringström's theorem for Bianchi IX), so beyond special classes such as Fournodavlos and Luk's no limiting residue exists; and the massless scalar is what makes singularities quiescent (Andersson and Rendall, 2001), precisely by allowing all exponents positive, which by (2) cannot be a unit boost. So, argued from the literature and not proved here, a generic non-diagonal extension of the forcing half cannot keep the unit-boost form: either no residue exists, or it is not a unit boost. Filed alongside, synthesis.nondiagonal-kasner-residue-weighted-shear places the residues of the non-diagonal class on the Kasner circle under the hypothesis that the slices' curvature is subleading; by (2) such a residue has an exponent $\leq 0$, the case in which that hypothesis generically fails (argued).
synthesis.unit-boost-residue-needs-nonpo.lay: Near a singularity of the Kasner type the geometry stretches in some directions and squeezes in others, at rates given by three exponents. The series showed that, in empty space, Einstein's equations make the singular part of the geometry a pure boost of unit size, and that this is exactly the input its completion needs. This result points out how special that is. The unit size requires one direction that does not stretch, which is also what makes empty-space singularities oscillate chaotically in general. Adding a simple kind of matter calms the oscillations, but then the boost is shorter than one. So the neat match the series found does not extend unchanged to generic singularities.

proofs.main:
\emph{(1)} In $\Cl(1,3)$ with $e_0^2 = 1$, $e_i^2 = -1$: $B_i^2 = e_0e_ie_0e_i = -e_0^2e_i^2 = 1$, and for $i 
eq j$, $B_iB_j = e_0e_ie_0e_j = -e_ie_j$, so $B_iB_j + B_jB_i = -(e_ie_j + e_je_i) = 0$. Hence $B_w^2 = \sum_i p_i^2 B_i^2 + \sum_{i<j}p_ip_j(B_iB_j + B_jB_i) = \sum_i p_i^2$, a scalar; checked exactly at two circle points and two disk points. With $\sum_i p_i = 1$ (the first Kasner relation, \claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-datum-kasner-wall}(ii)), $B_w^2 = 1$ is the second relation.

\emph{(2)} $1 = (\sum_i p_i)^2 = \sum_i p_i^2 + 2\sum_{i<j}p_ip_j$, so $\sum_i p_i^2 = 1 - 2\sum_{i<j}p_ip_j$. If every $p_i > 0$ the cross sum is positive and $\sum_i p_i^2 < 1$. On the circle the cross sum vanishes, so the exponents cannot all be positive: some $p_i \leq 0$. If $p_1 = 0$ on the circle then $p_2 + p_3 = 1 = p_2^2 + p_3^2$, so $p_2p_3 = 0$ and $p$ is a permutation of $(1,0,0)$. Checked: the rational parametrisation $p(u) = (-u, 1+u, u(1+u))/(1+u+u^2)$ satisfies both relations and has $p_1 < 0$ for $u > 0$; the zero-entry case on a grid; and every positive triple $(a,b,c)/12$ (55 of them) has $\sum p_i^2 < 1$, maximum $17/24$, with the cross-sum identity.

\emph{(3)} \claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-datum-kasner-wall}(ii) gives, in its convention (de Sitter has $\mathcal{R}(a) = \Lambda a$), the Ricci map $	au^2\mathcal{R}(e_0) = (\sum p_i^2 - \sum p_i)\,e_0$ and $	au^2\mathcal{R}(e_i) = p_i(\sum p_j - 1)\,e_i$ on the Kasner field with constant exponents (in components $	au^2R_{00} = \sum p_i^2 - \sum p_i$, $	au^2 R_{ii} = -p_i(\sum p_j - 1)$, the rest vanishing). In this convention a vacuum energy $T(a) = ho a$ with $ho = \Lambda/8\pi G$ has trace-reversed stress $-ho a$ and must produce $\mathcal{R}(a) = \Lambda a$, so the Einstein equation reads $\mathcal{R}(a) = -8\pi G\, igl(T(a) - 	frac12(\partial_b\cdot T(b))\,a igr)$. For a massless scalar the trace-reversed stress is $a \mapsto (a\cdot\hat
abla\phi)\,\hat
abla\phi$ in any signature, with $\hat
abla\phi = \hb^{T}(
abla\phi)$ the physical gradient (in components $\partial_a\phi\,\partial_b\phi$), and with $\phi = q\log	au$, $\hat
abla\phi = (q/	au)\,e_0$, so the right side is $-8\pi G\,q^2	au^{-2}e_0$ on $e_0$ and zero on each $e_i$. So $\mathcal{R}(e_i) = 0$, which for $p 
eq 0$ is $\sum p_i = 1$, and $\sum p_i^2 - 1 = -8\pi G q^2$. The wave equation $D\cdot\hat
abla\phi = 0$, in components $\Box\phi = 	au^{-\sum p_i}\partial_	au(	au^{\sum p_i}\partial_	au\phi) = 	au^{-1}\partial_	au(q) = 0$, holds exactly when $\sum p_i = 1$. The off-diagonal equations, $e_i\cdot\mathcal{R}(e_0)$, are those of \claimref{synthesis.diagonal-kasner-momentum-constraint} with the scalar's contribution $(e_0\cdot\hat
abla\phi)(e_i\cdot\hat
abla\phi) = 0$, so they are unchanged (constant exponents). Then $B_w^2 = \sum p_i^2 = 1 - 8\pi G q^2$ by (1). The isotropic stiff point $(	frac13,	frac13,	frac13)$, the stiff-fluid Friedmann expansion $a \propto 	au^{1/3}$, has $8\pi Gq^2 = 	frac23$. Checked: the relations at three points, including that the residue square equals $1 - 8\pi G q^2$ computed from $R_{00}$.

\emph{The last sentence.} Step (2) of \claimref{dark-energy.forcing-half-schwarzschild-wall-residue-sense} states that the residues satisfy the wall's field equations and that the second Kasner relation is the unit-boost property. By (3) the field equations at a wall with a scalar of nonzero log-rate give a residue of norm squared below one, so the equivalence holds only for $q = 0$, the vacuum case, and then (2) gives an exponent $p_i \leq 0$.

\emph{What is argued, not proved.} The dynamical reading in the technical level uses literature recalled from memory and not checked here: in vacuum, a Kasner regime with an exponent $p_1 < 0$ is destabilised by the spatial-curvature term growing like $	au^{4p_1}$ unless its structure constant vanishes (Belinski, Khalatnikov and Lifshitz, 1970; for Bianchi IX, Ringström, 2001, proved convergence to the oscillatory attractor), and the Fournodavlos-Luk class (2020) is built so that this term vanishes; with a massless scalar, solutions with all exponents positive are quiescent and exist in a full-dimensional family (Andersson and Rendall, 2001). These place the obstruction: a generic extension of the forcing half beyond the diagonal vacuum class either has no limiting residue or has a residue that is not a unit boost.
